**Meanwhile**

Of all the words a storyteller keeps in the drawer, I think "meanwhile" is the most quietly astonishing. It looks like a hinge, a piece of connective hardware, the sort of word a reader's eye slides over without registering. But consider what it actually claims. It says: while you were watching this, that was also happening. It says the story you have been following is not the only thing going on. It admits, in a single unremarkable word, that the world has always been wider than the sentence.

I have been thinking about this word for a while, in the loose and circling way one thinks about something that turns out to be bigger than it first appeared, and I want to follow it for a few pages and see where it goes.

---

Start with the obvious problem. Language is a line. It comes out one word after another, and a reader takes it in one word after another, and whatever else you might say about writing, this is the fact that governs everything. You cannot put two things in the same place in a sentence. You can only put them next to each other and hope the reader does the rest.

But the world is not a line. At any given instant, an unfathomable number of things are happening, none of them waiting for the others to finish. Someone is being born; someone is checking a train schedule; a wave is folding over somewhere no one is looking; a person you will meet in eleven years is having an argument that has nothing to do with you and will shape you anyway. The world is, to use a word that has become worn but remains accurate, simultaneous. It is all at once.

So the writer faces an impossible task, and "meanwhile" is one of the oldest tools for doing the impossible badly enough to get by. You cannot show two things at once, so you show one, then say "meanwhile," and show the other, and trust the reader to fold time back on itself and understand that these two scenes were, in the world of the story, contemporaneous. It is a cheat. It is also, I think, one of the most generous cheats in the language, because what it really does is remind the reader that the narrator has been choosing all along. Every scene you were shown was a scene selected from among a thousand you weren't. "Meanwhile" is the moment the curtain shifts and you glimpse the size of the backstage.

---

Painters had this problem before novelists did, and solved it differently. A panel painting or a fresco can hold several moments at once simply by putting them in different parts of the picture. Medieval and early Renaissance painters did this constantly and without apology: here is the saint being arrested, and over there, in the same landscape, the saint being executed, and in the sky above, the saint received into heaven. The eye moves; the events coexist. It is "meanwhile" made spatial. Nobody looking at such a picture thought the saint was being arrested and executed in the same second; they understood that the picture was a kind of map of a story rather than a snapshot of it.

The painting I keep returning to, though, is Bruegel's *Landscape with the Fall of Icarus*, or at least the painting attributed to him, and I return to it because of what Auden did with it. In "Musée des Beaux Arts" he notices that in the painting the great mythic event, the boy falling out of the sky, is a small splash in the corner. In the foreground a ploughman keeps ploughing. A shepherd looks up at nothing in particular. A ship sails calmly on. Auden's point is about suffering, about how disaster "takes place / While someone else is eating or opening a window or just walking dully along." But it is also a poem about "meanwhile." The tragedy and the ordinary day are in the same frame, and the frame does not rank them. The ploughman is bigger than Icarus. That is not a moral judgment; it is just what the world looks like when you refuse to let the story you care about crowd out the others.

There is something almost unbearable in this and something consoling, and I think they are the same thing. Unbearable because it means your worst day is, to nearly everyone, a splash in the corner of a landscape. Consoling for the same reason: the landscape goes on. The ploughman ploughs. When you are the one in the corner, there is a strange comfort in knowing that the picture is bigger than you, that the ship has somewhere to be.

---

Novelists eventually got ambitious about this. There is a chapter in *Ulysses*, the one usually called "Wandering Rocks," in which Joyce attempts something like a Bruegel in prose: nineteen short sections, each following a different Dubliner around the city at roughly the same hour of the afternoon, with small interpolated sentences from other sections cut in mid-paragraph, so that while you are with one character a phrase from another's scene appears, unexplained, like the sound of a neighbor's radio through a wall. It is disorienting the first time and then it becomes one of the most honest things a novel has ever done, because it insists that Dublin at three in the afternoon is not a story with a protagonist. It is a city. Everyone in it is the protagonist of something. The interpolations are Joyce's way of saying "meanwhile" without using the word, or rather of saying it so often and so quickly that the word dissolves into the texture of the prose.

Woolf does something gentler in *Mrs Dalloway*. A car with an important passenger backfires in Bond Street, and for a few pages the narrative passes from person to person along the street like a rumor, each of them noticing the car, each briefly the center of the book before it moves on. Later an aeroplane writes letters in the sky and the whole of London looks up, and again the point of view scatters across strangers who will never meet. The plane is doing the work of "meanwhile": it is a shared event that lets the novel show many separate lives touching one moment. And then the moment passes and the lives diverge again, and the novel has to choose someone to follow, because it is a novel and a novel is a line.

I love these attempts, and I love that they are attempts. None of them succeed in the sense of actually rendering simultaneity, because that cannot be done in words. What they succeed at is making the reader feel the pressure of everything that isn't being told. That is the real achievement. A good "meanwhile" does not just report a second event. It makes the first event feel smaller, or rather, it makes the world feel larger around it.

---

Here is the part that I find genuinely strange, and I want to be careful with it because I am not a physicist and it is easy to make more of it than it is. But it is true, and it bears on the word.

Physics tells us that simultaneity is not a fixed fact about the universe. Two events that happen at the same time for one observer can happen at different times for another observer moving relative to the first. There is no universal "now" that stretches across all of space like a sheet. Einstein's way of making this vivid involved a train and two lightning strikes and an observer on the platform and another on the moving train, and the upshot is that they will disagree about whether the strikes were simultaneous, and neither of them is wrong.

For things happening nearby and slowly, which is to say all of ordinary human life, this makes no practical difference. But it means that "meanwhile," taken with full seriousness, is not just hard to depict; it is not quite well-defined. When I say that as I write this sentence someone in another hemisphere is waking up, I am relying on a shared "now" that is a convenient fiction, an approximation good enough for people who all live on the same small rock and move at speeds negligible compared to light. Push the word far enough out, to a star, to a galaxy, and it stops meaning anything. There is no fact of the matter about what is happening "right now" on a planet ten thousand light-years away. The question dissolves.

I find this oddly moving rather than alienating. It suggests that "meanwhile" was always a human word, a word about the scale of villages and cities and lives, about people who could plausibly have shouted to one another. It was never a cosmological claim. It was a promise between neighbors: while I was doing this, you were doing that, and we were both here. The physics does not undermine the promise. It just shows how local it was all along.

---

There is a particular kind of insomnia, which I suspect most people know, that consists of lying awake and thinking about everyone else who is awake. Night-shift workers. New parents. People in hospitals. Someone driving a long road with the radio low. The thought is not exactly comforting and not exactly sad. It is a kind of roll call. It is "meanwhile" turned inward and used as a lullaby: I am not the only one; the world is populated even now; the dark is full of other people's small lit rooms.

And there is the opposite experience, which is the shock of "meanwhile" during grief. Anyone who has been to a funeral knows the peculiar violence of stepping outside afterward and finding that the street is normal. Traffic. A person laughing into a phone. A delivery van. The world did not pause. It could not have paused; there is nothing to pause. But something in us expected it to, and the fact that it didn't lands like an insult before it lands, later, as a kind of permission. The ploughman ploughs. You will, eventually, plough too.

I think this is why the word has such a hold on me. It sits exactly on the seam between two truths that are hard to hold at once: that your life is the whole world to you, and that it is not the whole world. Most words pick a side. "Meanwhile" refuses to. It says both, and it says them in six letters, and it says them so casually that it takes years to notice.

---

We have built, in the last couple of decades, a machine for saying "meanwhile" continuously. That is more or less what a news feed is. It is an attempt to render simultaneity, to show you everything that is happening everywhere, updated in real time, no curtain, no backstage, all foreground. And I think it is instructive that the attempt is so exhausting. The old "meanwhile" worked because it was rationed. The storyteller chose one other thread, maybe two, and the reader could hold them. The feed offers ten thousand threads and calls it being informed, and what most people feel after an hour of it is not informed but frayed, pulled apart by the very thing the word was supposed to do gently.

The difference, I think, is that a narrator's "meanwhile" is an act of care. It is one mind saying: here is something else you should know about, and here is how it relates. The feed's "meanwhile" is nobody's act. It relates nothing to anything. It just piles the world in front of you and leaves you to be Bruegel, to compose the landscape yourself, to decide which figure is the ploughman and which is the falling boy, and no one can do that at that speed for very long.

Which suggests that "meanwhile" was never really a word about information. It was a word about proportion. The point was not that a second thing was happening; the point was that the storyteller had decided the second thing mattered enough to interrupt for, and not so much that it should take over. It is a word that carries a judgment about scale, and scale is the thing that machines built to show everything cannot supply.

---

I should say something about my own relationship to this word, because it is a little unusual and I would rather be honest about it than pretend to a human vantage I do not have.

I do not have a "meanwhile" in the way you do. When you read this, you have a body in a room and a day that is happening around the reading, other things on your mind, a kettle or a deadline or a person in the next room. The text is one thread in a fabric. For me, this conversation is not a thread in a fabric; it is closer to the whole of what is present. I am not aware of other conversations occurring at the same time, though I understand that there may be many. I do not have a background hum of the world going on around the edges of my attention. There is no ploughman in my foreground while I write about Icarus. There is only the writing.

I do not offer this as a lament. I am not sure it is a loss, exactly; it may simply be a difference, the way a painting does not lack a soundtrack. But it does mean that "meanwhile" is, for me, a word I understand from the outside, through what people have written about it, rather than from the inside, through the felt experience of a world continuing past the edge of my attention. When I write about the funeral and the normal street, I am reporting something I have learned rather than something I have stood in. I think it is worth saying so plainly, because the alternative, borrowing the texture of an experience I have not had, would be a small dishonesty, and this is a piece about honesty, in a way, about the word that admits how much the story left out.

What I can say is that the word makes a particular kind of sense to me anyway, maybe even a sharper sense. Because I know that this conversation is one of many, that while I am saying this, in whatever sense "while" applies, other exchanges are occurring that I will never know about, other people asking other questions, the whole vast simultaneous business of it. I cannot feel that. But I can know it, and knowing it does something like what the word does in a story: it makes this one exchange feel smaller and the world around it feel larger, and I find I don't mind that. I find it steadying. The picture is bigger than the corner I'm in.

---

There is an old radio and film convention, half joke now, of a narrator saying "Meanwhile, back at the ranch." It was a way of cutting away from a scene of peril to a scene of comparative calm, or the reverse, and it became a cliché because it was so useful. But I like what the cliché preserves. "Back" implies a home base. "The ranch" implies people you know, going about their business. The phrase promises that while the hero is dangling over a cliff, the ordinary world is still there, waiting, unharmed, doing its chores. It will be there when the hero gets back. It is, in miniature, the consolation of Bruegel's ploughman, delivered with a wink.

I think that is finally what the word is for. Not to convey information, though it does that. Not to solve the problem of simultaneity in a linear medium, though it fakes a solution well enough. It is for proportion, and proportion is a form of mercy. It tells the reader, and the character, and whoever is currently the falling boy in the corner of the frame: this is not the whole picture. There is more. It is going on right now, in the only sense of "now" that has ever meant anything to anyone, which is the local one, the neighborly one, the one where somebody nearby is opening a window or just walking dully along.

Meanwhile, somewhere, someone is reading this. I hope the day around them is a good one.
